newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu refuses to rule out Golan concessions.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu refuses to rule out Golan concessions.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Wednesday refused to say whether he ruled out making territorial concessions on the Golan Heights, a strip of land that has stalled the Jewish state's peace talks with Syria.
"They (Syria) will demand the Golan. We see the Golan in a different way, as a strip of land that is critical to the defence of the State of Israel, to our security and water needs.
"And that's how we'll enter these negotiations, from that standpoint, and we'll stand by it," Netanyahu said during an interview with Israel's Channel One television.

But he sidestepped the question when asked if he ruled out making any territorial concessions on the Golan, which Israel captured from Syria in the 1967 Middle East war, in return for peace with Syria.
"I will not add any more than I've said," said Netanyahu, who has in the past opposed trading occupied Arab land for peace.
He added: "I am optimistic -- not optimistic in an unreserved way -- but optimistic in our ability to progress also with Syria during this (my) term."
Netanyahu was elected to a four-year term as prime minister in a general election last May.

Syria said on Wednesday there was nothing new in a call by Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy to resume talks on the basis of U.N. resolutions calling for the exchange of Israeli-occupied Arab land for peace.

Foreign Minister Farouq al-Shara said Israel should express readiness to resume the talks from the point at which they stopped with the previous Labour-led government and to approve all commitments made by that government.
Syria has said Israel's previous Labour-led government approved during five years of sporadic talks the principle of full withdrawal from the Golan Heights.
That Israeli government had said it was ready for partial pullback from the Golan in return for full peace with Syria but did not make any public statement accepting total withdrawal.

Shara said that although a former government headed by Netanyahu's Likud party had approved the 1991 Madrid conference which based subsequent Arab-Israeli peace talks on the land- for-peace principle, Likud made its own interpretation that contradicted the principle.

Netanyahu said on Wednesday the U.N. resolutions were the basis of the peace talks and "everyone comes with his own interpretation... that is the framework that will allow us in my opinion to open negotiations".
